paragraphs.text: # One Ticket to Win Them All — Figure 2 evidence slice
### 4.1 Transfer within the same data distribution
As a first test of whether winning tickets generalize, we investigate the simplest form of transfer: generalization across samples drawn from the same data distribution. To measure this, we divided

**Figure 2:** Transferring winning tickets within the same data distribution. CIFAR-10 was divided into two halves ("10a" and "10b"), each of which contained 25,000 total examples with 2,500 images per class. Winning tickets generated using CIFAR-10a generalized well to CIFAR-10b for both VGG19 (a) and ResNet50 (b). Error bars represent mean ± standard deviation across six random seeds.

the CIFAR-10 dataset into two halves: CIFAR-10a and CIFAR-10b. Each half contained 25,000 training images with 2,500 images per class. We then asked whether winning tickets generated using CIFAR-10a would produce increased performance on CIFAR-10b. To evaluate the impact of transferring a winning ticket, we compared the CIFAR-10a ticket to both a random ticket and to a winning ticket generated on CIFAR-10b itself (Figure 2). Interestingly, for ResNet50 models, while both CIFAR-10a and CIFAR-10b winning tickets outperformed random tickets at extreme pruning fractions, both under-performed random tickets at low pruning fractions, suggesting that ResNet winning tickets may be particularly sensitive to smaller datasets at low pruning fractions.

related_claims.content: A winning ticket discovered on CIFAR-10a (a subset of the CIFAR-10 dataset containing 25,000 training images with 2,500 images per class), transfers to a disjoint subset CIFAR-10b from the same data distribution and improves training on that held-out subset relative to random sparse initializations.

The within-distribution transfer described in claim 12 holds for both VGG19 and ResNet50. [Referenced claim 12: A winning ticket discovered on CIFAR-10a (a subset of the CIFAR-10 dataset containing 25,000 training images with 2,500 images per class), transfers to a disjoint subset CIFAR-10b from the same data distribution and improves training on that held-out subset relative to random sparse initializations.]
ResNet50 showed sensitivity at low pruning fractions, occasionally under-performing random tickets when few weights are pruned.

equivalent_claims.content: On CIFAR-10b with ResNet50, at extreme pruning fractions, both types of winning tickets—those produced on CIFAR-10a and those produced on CIFAR-10b—achieve better performance than random tickets; the error bars correspond to mean ± standard deviation across six random seeds.

On CIFAR-10b with ResNet50, at low pruning fractions, both types of winning tickets—those produced on CIFAR-10a and those produced on CIFAR-10b—achieve worse performance than random tickets; the error bars correspond to mean ± standard deviation across six random seeds.

When CIFAR-10 is divided into 10a and 10b, each consisting of 25,000 training images (2,500 per class), winning tickets produced on CIFAR-10a generalize effectively to CIFAR-10b for VGG19 and ResNet50; the error bars correspond to mean ± standard deviation across six random seeds.
